algorithm.Title: Rash - Widespread On Drugs - Female (Child)
algorithm.ContentSet: IST Open-Source Guideline Content | Child | Female
Definition: Suspected medication-related widespread rash assessment decomposed from NHS.UK's published rash emergency guidance.

Background.ExpertReviewer: PENDING: Qatar pediatric, emergency, allergy, dermatology, pharmacy, safeguarding, and nursing governance review

FirstAid: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive. If anaphylaxis is suspected, use the child's prescribed adrenaline auto-injector immediately according to its instructions and emergency plan; antihistamine must not delay adrenaline or 999. Do not give another dose of the suspected medicine unless 999/qualified prescriber explicitly directs it, and do not give food, drink, or oral medicine if swallowing or responsiveness is impaired. Keep all packaging and a medicine list for handover. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.

questions.Question: Are throat or tongue swelling, breathing difficulty, faintness, confusion, or collapse the main concern?
questions.Information: Systemic allergic-reaction features require the anaphylaxis pathway rather than an isolated rash pathway.

questions.Question: Is there lip/mouth/throat/tongue swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, faintness, confusion, unusual floppiness, or collapse; a purple/non-fading rash with illness; or fever with painful skin, blisters, peeling, rapidly spreading redness, facial swelling, or sores involving the mouth, eyes, or genitals?
questions.Information: Airway, breathing, circulation, or responsiveness change may indicate anaphylaxis. Non-fading rash with illness may indicate sepsis, while painful blistering/peeling or mucosal involvement after medicine exposure may represent a severe cutaneous adverse reaction; all require emergency assessment.

questions.Question: With every emergency feature excluded, is there a new widespread rash after any medicine, supplement, traditional remedy, vaccine/injection, or dose change?
questions.Information: A rash appearing soon after starting a new medication warrants prompt review to assess whether the medication should be stopped, even without the source's own listed emergency signs.

advice.Title: Qatar emergency medicine-rash response
Content: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive. If anaphylaxis is suspected, use the child's prescribed adrenaline auto-injector immediately according to its instructions and emergency plan; antihistamine must not delay adrenaline or 999. Do not give another dose of the suspected medicine unless 999/qualified prescriber explicitly directs it, and do not give food, drink, or oral medicine if swallowing or responsiveness is impaired. Keep all packaging and a medicine list for handover. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.

Call Back If: airway swelling, breathing difficulty, faintness, floppiness, or collapse; non-fading rash with illness; painful skin, blistering, peeling, mucosal sores, facial swelling, fever, or rapid progression.

advice.Title: Urgent pediatric medication-rash review
Content: Arrange prompt same-day in-person pediatric assessment through the Qatar route approved by governance and contact an authorized prescriber/pharmacist before the next dose when this can be done without delaying care. Do not independently restart, substitute, or permanently discontinue an essential medicine; document the suspected product as a reaction, not a confirmed allergy, until assessed. Do not use leftover antihistamine, steroid, antibiotic, or topical treatment without age/weight and interaction checks. Call 999 immediately for any emergency feature.
Call Back If: rash spreads, becomes painful, blisters, peels, or involves mouth/eyes/genitals; fever, facial swelling, breathing/swallowing change, faintness, or floppiness.

references: NHS.UK, "Skin rash in children", https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/skin-rash-children/ (page last reviewed 03 October 2024)

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: What is the child's exact age, sex, weight, allergies and medical conditions, and what prescribed, over-the-counter, traditional/herbal, or injected medicine was started, stopped, or changed? Record exact name, dose, timing, last dose, and packaging if safely available.

initialAssessmentQuestions.Question: Where is the rash and how fast is it spreading? Ask about facial/airway swelling, breathing/swallowing, faintness/floppiness, fever, pain, purple/non-fading spots, blisters/peeling, skin tenderness, mouth/eye/genital sores, facial swelling, vomiting, reduced urine, and safeguarding or dosing-error concerns.
